docs.title: User guide
docs.text: This guide shows how to sign in, start a GPU workspace, manage projects and groups, use storage, and ask administrators for more.

docs.title: What you can do
docs.text:
• Launch GPU workspaces (JupyterLab or VS Code) with persistent storage
  • Open a GPU desktop or Isaac Sim session in the browser
  • Manage projects: GPU/CPU/memory quotas, versioned config files, members
  • Work in groups with shared storage and roles
  • Submit requests for resources, storage, or image access
  • Read announcements about maintenance and policy changes
  • Watch your quota usage and running GPU jobs on the Home dashboard

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A current browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari)
  • An account created by a platform administrator
  • VPN access if the platform runs on a private network

docs.title: First steps
docs.text:
Follow the Getting started guide from VPN setup to your first workspace.

First-time checklist

  • [ ] Connect to the VPN
  • [ ] Sign in at https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  • [ ] Look at the Home dashboard
  • [ ] Check your project's GPU quota under Projects
  • [ ] Launch a workspace

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role What it can do User Use resources within the project's quota Manager Manage projects and groups; limited admin pages Admin Everything, including all admin pages

See Concepts and roles for the full permission tables.

docs.title: Announcements
docs.text:
Announcements are platform-wide messages from administrators. They appear as dashboard banners and stay on the Announcements page until they expire. Scheduled announcements stay hidden until their publish time.

Access: All authenticated users.

docs.title: Where Announcements Appear
docs.text:
Location What You See Home Dashboard Pinned or unread announcements appear near the top of the page. Sidebar → Announcements Full list of active announcements with All and Unread filters. Modal view Full title, content, priority, publish date, and expiry date. Sign-in popup Unread critical announcements open automatically when you sign in (or reload), one at a time, until you click Got it. Notification bell The bell in the header counts unread announcements and lists the latest three above your notifications.

Announcements can have info, warning, or critical priority. Critical notices usually describe maintenance, service degradation, or actions users must take.

docs.title: Read and Acknowledge
docs.text:
1. Open Announcements from the sidebar, or click View all on a dashboard banner.
  2. Select an announcement to open the detail modal.
  3. Opening an unread announcement marks it as read for your account.

Critical announcements also appear as a popup at sign-in. Got it marks the announcement read; closing the popup with ✕ only hides it for this session, so it shows again next time you sign in.

Pinned announcements may continue to appear even after you read them, until an administrator unpins or expires them.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
Why did an announcement disappear?

The announcement probably reached its expiry time or was removed by an administrator.

Can I reply to an announcement?

No. Use Requests if you need help or want to ask about a notice.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
Use cscc-cli to authenticate, submit image builds, stream build logs, and manage your own API tokens.

Access: All authenticated users.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
On a new machine, give the CLI the API URL explicitly with --api-url or CSCC_API_URL. The value may include /api/v1; the CLI normalizes it for you.

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

The CLI prompts for your password. Unlike the dashboard, this flow needs no CAPTCHA.

On success, the CLI saves a cscc_... API token in its local config file, readable only by you. The token value itself is shown only once when it is created.

Optional token name:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice --name workstation

Token names are limited to 100 characters. Leave the flag off to use the default name, cscc-cli.

docs.title: Import a dashboard-created token
docs.text:
You can also create an API token from Settings → API Key & CLI in the dashboard and import it into cscc-cli:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --token cscc_...

The CLI verifies the token before saving it. This is handy when you are already signed in to the dashboard and would rather not type your password in a terminal.

docs.title: Stateless token override
docs.text:
For automation, set CSCC_API_TOKEN instead of saving local config:

CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw CSCC_API_TOKEN=cscc_... cscc-cli whoami

CSCC_DEV_TOKEN is still accepted as a deprecated compatibility alias, but new scripts should use CSCC_API_TOKEN.

docs.title: TLS / Internal CA
docs.text:
Official cscc-cli releases already trust the platform's certificate, so most users never need to configure one. If the platform certificate is rotated, download the latest CLI release before reconnecting.

The variables below are only for custom builds and TLS troubleshooting:

Env Description CSCC_API_URL API base URL, e.g. https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw/api/v1 CSCC_API_TOKEN Optional stateless cscc_... token override CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH One or multiple PEM files separated by , or ; CSCC_API_TLS_SERVER_NAME Optional TLS SNI name (fallback to config if not set) SSL_CERT_FILE Path to a PEM file containing the internal root CA REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE Alternative env path for a PEM bundle containing the internal root CA

Example:

CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH=/Users/me/platform-internal-root-ca.pem \
  cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

docs.title: Check Identity
docs.text:
cscc-cli whoami

This verifies the saved token and prints your current user and role. Role changes take effect immediately.

docs.title: Build Images
docs.text:
Upload mode is the default and accepts a directory, a .tar.gz, or a .zip archive:

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1.0.1 .
cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer ./context.tar.gz

For directories, the CLI packs the target directory into a .tar.gz build context. The context or uploaded archive must contain a root-level Dockerfile.

Dockerfile-only mode matches the dashboard's pasted-Dockerfile flow:

cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --tag v1.0.1 \
  --dockerfile ./Dockerfile

cat Dockerfile | cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --dockerfile -

Useful options:

Option Description --project Project ID that owns the image build --name Short image name, for example trainer-api --tag Optional image tag. Omit it to use the platform default --source upload or dockerfile --dockerfile Dockerfile path, or - for stdin, when --source dockerfile --build-arg Dockerfile ARG override as KEY=VALUE; repeatable --follow=false Submit the build without streaming logs

docs.title: Build arguments
docs.text:
Pass Dockerfile ARG values at build time with --build-arg KEY=VALUE. The flag is repeatable and works with upload and dockerfile builds. Each KEY must start with a letter or underscore and contain only letters, digits, and underscores.

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1 \
  --build-arg HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \
  --build-arg MAX_JOBS=4 \
  .

Use this to keep secrets and tunables out of the committed Dockerfile (for example an ARG HF_TOKEN), or to cap compile parallelism (MAX_JOBS, FLASH_ATTN_MAX_JOBS, …) so a heavy build fits the shared build engine.

Build args are visible to anyone who can inspect the build. Treat them as low-sensitivity, and rotate any token passed this way once the build is done.

docs.title: Shared build queue
docs.text:
Image builds share one build engine and run one at a time. Each build gets a fixed amount of CPU, memory, and scratch space that you cannot override.

After submission, --follow=true (the default) waits for logs to become available, streams them, and exits once the build reports completed, failed, or deleted.

The CLI takes the API endpoint from --api-url at login, then CSCC_API_URL, then its saved config:

export CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw

Builds and log streams use the token created by cscc-cli login — no other credential is needed. The project must have Image Build Permission enabled, and your project role must allow builds.

docs.title: Token Management
docs.text:
List active API tokens:

cscc-cli tokens list

Revoke a token by ID:

cscc-cli tokens revoke <token-id>

Log out from the current machine:

cscc-cli logout

Logout revokes the token in use and clears it from local config. Any manual certificate settings are kept so you can log in again without redoing them.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes Token lifetime 90 days Create a new token when the old one expires Active tokens per user 20 Revoke unused tokens if you hit the limit Failed sign-ins before lockout 5 Applies to both the dashboard and the CLI Lockout duration 15 min Wait it out, or ask an admin to unlock the account

Your administrator can adjust these values for the deployment.

docs.title: Concepts & Roles
docs.text: Understanding the platform's tenancy model and permission system helps you work effectively with projects, groups, and storage.

docs.title: Tenancy Hierarchy
docs.text:
A group holds projects; a project launches workspaces and binds storage.

Entity Description Group A team or department. Groups own shared storage and can be project members. Project The primary resource allocation unit. Holds GPU/CPU quotas, config files, and deployments. Workspace An interactive IDE (JupyterLab / VSCode) running inside the project's quota. Storage volume Persistent storage; survives workspace restarts.

docs.title: Quota Lifecycle
docs.text:
Each project is assigned a Resource Plan by an admin. When you launch a workspace, the platform checks the project quota and your per-user quota before reserving anything.

A plan also carries:

  • An allowed GPU model list — only these models are selectable from the launch form.
  • An optional schedule window that restricts when plan-bound queues are usable (see Plan Window below).
  • One or more bound queues with their priority, preemption, and GPU-model policy.

docs.title: Scheduling Queues, Priority, and Preemption
docs.text:
Workloads choose a scheduling queue. A queue owns a priority value, an optional preemptible flag, and an optional deserved GPU limit:

Concept Meaning Priority Higher-priority queues are scheduled first when GPUs are scarce. Preemptible Workloads in this queue can be stopped to free GPUs for higher-priority queues. Deserved GPU The GPU floor a queue is guaranteed even when other queues compete. A 0 value marks a queue as a "victim" eligible to be drained first.

The default queue is always available; plan-bound queues are listed alongside it on the workspace and deploy forms.

docs.title: Plan Window
docs.text:
A plan window is the time interval during which a project's plan-bound queues are usable. Outside the window, those queues stop accepting new workloads and may stop the ones already running. Workloads on the default queue are not affected.

The dashboard shows live countdowns for the next boundary (open/close). When a window has closed, the deploy dialog offers Switch to Default Queue; this applies to deployments only. A workspace cannot change queue; create a new one inside the next window.

docs.title: GPU Claims
docs.text:
Every GPU on the platform is handed out through a claim. A claim describes:

  • A GPU model
  • An SM share percentage — how much of that GPU's compute you get
  • A VRAM policy — elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads, hard cap enforces a strict ceiling

There are two kinds:

  • Inline claim — created automatically when you launch a workspace. It lives and dies with that workspace.
  • Project GPU claim — created from a project's GPU Claims tab and reused across deployments. It reserves GPU quota as soon as you create it, but only accrues GPU-hours while a workload is actually attached.

A project config file refers to a project GPU claim through a named claim slot (for example train-a). The slot name is only a label — you map it to one of your own claims in the deploy dialog. Every replica of a Deployment shares the same claim and is counted once, so split the workload into separate Deployments if only some replicas should use one.

docs.title: GPU-Hour Budget
docs.text:
A resource plan can also cap the cumulative GPU time a project consumes, on top of the concurrent GPU/CPU/memory limits above. One GPU-hour is one allocated GPU running for one hour; a fractional GPU counts the same fraction.

The budget resets on a window an administrator sets per project — monthly by default, or weekly, or every fixed number of hours. Your project's Overview tab shows usage against the budget for the current window and when it next resets. Once the budget is used up, new GPU jobs and workspaces are blocked until the reset; jobs already running keep going.

docs.text: Permission User Manager Admin Use workspaces within quota ✓ ✓ ✓ Create personal projects ✓ ✓ ✓ Submit resource requests ✓ ✓ ✓ Access admin panel ✓ ✓ Manage all users / groups ✓ Define resource plans ✓ Manage platform queues ✓ View audit logs ✓ ✓ Role and permission management ✓

docs.title: Storage Permission Model
docs.text:
Storage permissions follow two paths:

  • Group storage permissions are the source of truth. Group members always inherit them; the project cannot override them.
  • The project Storage page shows inherited permissions read-only.
  • To change a group member's access, edit it on the group page. Project members who are not in the group are managed on the project page; users outside the project cannot receive project-level storage grants.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Storage volume Persistent storage that survives workspace restarts Scheduling Queue A named policy that controls priority, preemption, queue windows, and optional GPU model affinity Plan Window The time interval during which a project's plan-bound queues are usable Preemption Stopping a workload in a preemptible queue so a higher-priority one can run GPU Claim A GPU reservation. Project claims reserve quota when created and accrue GPU-hours only while a workload is attached GPU-hour One allocated GPU running for one hour. A plan's GPU-hour budget caps the cumulative total a project may consume in its reset window (monthly by default, set per project) Config File A versioned deployment definition; every save creates a new, immutable version SM share The percentage of a GPU's compute you are allocated Resource Plan A named template defining GPU, CPU, memory limits, allowed GPU models, and schedule windows for a project Workspace An interactive cloud IDE (JupyterLab, VSCode)

docs.title: GPU desktops
docs.text:
A GPU desktop is a remote desktop that runs on a platform GPU and opens in your browser: a Linux desktop for GUI tools, or an Isaac Sim session streamed live. You get a window, keyboard, and mouse; the GPU stays in the cluster.

Access: members of a project where an admin has turned on Remote Desktop Permission. If none of your projects has it, the page says Remote Desktop is not enabled for any of your projects and you ask an administrator.

docs.title: Where to find it
docs.text:
• Sidebar → Workspace → GPU Desktops lists every desktop session across your projects, in any state, not only the ones you can connect to.
  • A desktop is not created on this page. It comes from a project config file, the same way as a deployment; see Start a desktop below.

docs.title: Start a desktop
docs.text:
Starting a desktop needs the Manager role in the project (the same as deploying a config file).

  1. Open Projects → [your project] → Config and click New File.
  2. In the Resource Wizard, add a Pod (or Deployment with one replica) with one container and its image, CPU, and memory.
  3. Turn on the Remote desktop switch under the container. The platform replaces this workload with an isolated browser desktop; the image itself is not rebuilt.
  4. Fill in the desktop fields:
Field What to choose Desktop type Linux desktop (your image, with a desktop drawn around it) or Isaac Sim WebRTC (the platform's Isaac Sim image, streamed) GPU device class The GPU model GPU reservation 25% GPU, 50% GPU, 75% GPU, or 100% GPU. Below 100% the card is shared with others; 100% is exclusive Bitrate profile Economy, Default, or High motion. Economy is the right choice off campus
  1. Click Save, then Deploy the version as usual (pick a queue; the plan window applies).
  2. Go to GPU Desktops. The row appears with its status; when it shows Ready, click Connect.

Rules for a remote-desktop workload

  • One container, one replica, and no GPU request or GPU claim of its own; the desktop fields above replace them.
  • Isaac Sim WebRTC needs the platform's Isaac Sim image, one exclusive GPU, and the VPN. Mount exactly one storage volume, read-write and at /workspace, and nothing else. Set CPU and memory yourself within the project quota; one session measured about 10 cores and 19 GB.
  • Mounted volumes must be storage volumes (personal or group); other volume types are rejected.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Status What it means What you can do Pending Waiting for a GPU and encoder slot Wait Starting The desktop is being set up Wait Ready Running and reachable Connect Degraded Running, with a caveat shown in the row (for example software encoding, slower and heavier on CPU) Connect still works Failed Could not start Delete, then deploy again Stopping Being removed Wait Expired Its lifetime ran out Delete, then deploy again when you need it

Each row shows the desktop name, project, GPU model, encoder, image, and the expiry time, with a status badge for its current state. Any row that isn't Ready shows a reason when one is available (red for Failed, amber otherwise). A desktop whose image has no graphical libraries cannot be opened; the row has no Connect button. Failed and Expired rows have a Delete button.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
• Linux desktop: Connect opens the desktop in a new browser window.
  • Isaac Sim WebRTC: Connect opens the viewer at GPU Desktops → [desktop]. Click the stream to take keyboard and mouse control; Leave control gives them back to the browser, Full screen fills the screen. Stay on the VPN: if the viewer says VPN media authorization expired, reconnect the VPN and reload the page.

The viewer renews its connection every 2 minutes while open. Closing the tab does not stop the desktop.

docs.title: Lifetime
docs.text:
• A desktop lives at most 8 hours, or less if the project's Max workspace continuous runtime (Settings tab) or the queue's runtime limit is shorter. The row shows the expiry time.
  • A desktop nobody is watching for 30 minutes is reclaimed to free the GPU.
  • When it expires, files in the mounted storage volume stay; everything else in the desktop is gone. Deploy the config file again to get a fresh desktop.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The GPU Desktops page is empty.

No desktop is running in your projects. Deploy a config file with Remote desktop turned on (see Start a desktop). If the page says Remote Desktop is not enabled, ask an admin to turn it on for the project.

The status stays Pending.

The desktop is waiting for a free GPU slice or video encoder. It starts when one frees up; 100% reservations wait for a whole free card.

The row says Degraded. Is it broken?

No. It runs, but with the caveat shown in the row, usually software encoding on a node without a hardware encoder. Connect works; expect more latency.

Where are my files?

Only the mounted storage volume survives the desktop. For Isaac Sim that is /workspace. Save there.

Can I keep the desktop for more than 8 hours?

No. Deploy again after it expires; the mounted volume is the same, so your work is still there.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
A step-by-step guide to connecting, signing in, launching your first GPU workspace, and deploying a container.

Access: All users with a platform account provisioned by an administrator.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Details Browser Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari (latest version) Account Username and password provided by your platform admin VPN client OpenVPN-compatible client (see Step 1 below)

VPN is required

The platform runs on a private network. Connect via OpenVPN first, then use the DNS names under cscc.nthu.edu.tw; do not browse raw infrastructure URLs.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install a VPN client
docs.text: OS Recommended client Install Windows OpenVPN Connect Download installer from the official site macOS Tunnelblick or OpenVPN Connect brew install --cask tunnelblick Linux OpenVPN CLI sudo apt install openvpn or sudo dnf install openvpn

docs.title: Step 2 — Connect to the VPN
docs.text:
1. Get the VPN profile (Platform-VPN.ovpn) from your administrator.
  2. Import it into your VPN client:
    • Windows / macOS GUI: drag the .ovpn file onto the client window, or use Import Profile.
    • Linux CLI: sudo openvpn --config Platform-VPN.ovpn
  3. When prompted, enter your platform username and password (the same credentials you use to sign in).
  4. Wait for the connection to establish. The client shows a green indicator or Initialization Sequence Completed.

Verify connectivity

Open a terminal and run: 

nslookup dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
If the name resolves and the dashboard opens, you are connected. If not, check that UDP port 31194 is not blocked by your firewall.

Windows route check

If OpenVPN shows connected but 192.168.109.1 is unreachable, open PowerShell and run route print | findstr 192.168.109. The output should include a 192.168.109.0 route through the OpenVPN adapter. If it is missing, re-import the latest Platform-VPN.ovpn.

The VPN profile pushes the platform DNS server for cscc.nthu.edu.tw and turns on block-outside-dns, so Windows uses only that DNS server while connected. Use Resolve-DnsName dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw to confirm platform DNS and http://192.168.109.1:30080 for low-level connectivity checks.

docs.title: Step 3 — Sign in to the platform
docs.text:
1. Open your browser and navigate to: 
    https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  2. The login page has three fields:
Field Description Username Your platform account username Password Your platform account password CAPTCHA Type the 4-digit number shown in the image
  1. Fill in all three fields and click SIGN IN.

Figure 1: Login page with username, password, and CAPTCHA fields.

CAPTCHA

Click the CAPTCHA image to refresh it if it is hard to read.

docs.title: Step 4 — Explore the Home Dashboard
docs.text:
After login you land on the Home Dashboard at /.

Widget What it shows Platform GPU Available Free vs. allocated GPU units across the platform GPU Cluster Status Anonymised GPU node cards showing how much of each GPU is in use Project count (header line) How many projects you belong to, and how many of them have a plan Resource Usage History Live quota usage for each project that has a plan Recent Activity Your recent requests My GPU Jobs Your running GPU jobs with GPU share, memory, and running time

Figure 2: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, GPU cluster status, and My GPU Jobs.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check your project
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Projects in the left sidebar (Workspace section).
  2. A personal project is auto-created when your account is provisioned. Look for a project named after your username.
  3. Click the project card to view its quota (GPU, CPU, Memory limits) and members.

Figure 3: Projects page showing personal project card with quota summary.

No project visible?

Ask your administrator to assign you to a project or group, or check that your account has been fully provisioned.

docs.title: Step 6 — Launch your first workspace
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Workspaces in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Workspace.
  3. Fill in the launch form:
Field What to choose Project Select your project (personal or team) Environment JupyterLab or VS Code Image One of the platform's images: Base Notebook, PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA Dev, or a "(Root)" variant CPU Number of CPU cores (e.g., 2) Memory RAM in GB (e.g., 8) GPU Number of GPUs Compute quota (%) Share of each GPU's compute; 100% is a full GPU GPU memory quota (%) Share of each GPU's memory; leave Follow compute on to match the compute quota Storage Volumes Tick the volumes to mount. Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>, group volumes at /mnt/shared/<volume name>
  1. Click Start.
  2. Wait for the status badge to change from Starting (yellow) → Running (green).
  3. Click Open. Your IDE opens in a new browser tab.

Figure 4: Workspace creation form with project, IDE type, and resource fields.

Workspace won't start?

  • Verify your project has sufficient quota remaining.
  • Check if the scheduling plan window is currently active (ask your admin).
  • GPU images take longer to download on first launch.

docs.title: Step 7 — Deploy a container
docs.text:
A workspace gives you an interactive IDE. When you want to run your own container image instead (a long-running service or a batch job), deploy a container from a project config file. Config files can define Pod, Deployment, and Job workloads.

Requires Project Manager role

Creating and deploying config files needs the Manager role or higher. You already have this in your personal project; for a team project, ask a project manager.

  1. Go to Projects → [your project] → Config tab.
  2. Click New File. Paste a YAML manifest, or use the built-in Resource Wizard to fill in the fields without hand-writing YAML.

  3. Define your container:

    Field What to set Image A container image from the platform allowlist; see Requests to add a new one CPU / Memory Set both requests and limits; memory must be at least 128Mi (e.g. 512Mi) GPU (optional) Add a GPU request such as nvidia.com/rtx6000: "1", or map a reusable GPU claim Storage (optional) Use {{userVolume}} to mount your personal storage volume

  4. Click Save. Each save creates a new, immutable version.

    Figure 5: The Config tab: creating a new config with the Resource Wizard.

  5. On the version row, click Deploy.

  6. In the deploy dialog, choose a scheduling queue. If your YAML uses GPU claim slots, map each slot to one of your reserved claims. You can click Dry-run first to validate without consuming quota.

  7. Click Deploy, then watch the instance until it shows Running. Open logs or status from the instance view to check on it.

    Figure 6: The deploy dialog: choosing a scheduling queue and GPU claim.

Deploy rejected?

  • Every container must set both resources.requests.memory and resources.limits.memory (≥ 128Mi); missing values are rejected.
  • The image must be on the platform allowlist. Submit an image request first if it is not.
  • Leave metadata.namespace out; the platform fills it in.
  • Deploying needs the Manager role and enough remaining project quota.

For config-file versioning, GPU requests, and reusable GPU claims in depth, see Projects → Config File Versioning.

docs.title: Step 8 — Manage your storage
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Storage in the left sidebar (Resources section). The My Storage tab opens.
  2. Click Start FileBrowser.
  3. Click Open FileBrowser. A FileBrowser window opens where you can upload, download, rename, and organise files.
  4. Files stored here persist across workspaces. Click Stop FileBrowser when you are done.

Figure 7: FileBrowser interface showing personal storage contents.

docs.title: Step 9 — Join a group (optional)
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Groups in the left sidebar.
  2. Browse available groups or ask your admin to add you.
  3. Group members share a group storage volume, useful for datasets and shared models.
  4. Group managers can set per-user permissions (Read / Write / None) on shared storage.

docs.title: Service quick reference
docs.text:
Regular users only need the platform dashboard. Other service hostnames are reserved for the CLI, integrations, and administrators.

Service URL Purpose Dashboard https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw Main platform UI for users

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
VPN connects but dashboard DNS does not resolve

Make sure your VPN client accepts the DNS settings from the profile. Some clients require enabling DNS update scripts or importing the profile again. The user-facing entrypoint is https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw.

CAPTCHA is wrong but I typed it correctly

The code is 4 digits. If the image is unclear, click it to get a new code.

Login fails with 'Invalid credentials'

Verify you are using your username, not your email address. If your password was changed recently, the old one stops working immediately.

Workspace stuck in 'Starting' state

This usually means the container image is being downloaded for the first time (this can take several minutes for large GPU images). If it stays in Starting for more than 10 minutes, check with your admin that the scheduling queue is active and your project's plan window is open.

Session expired and redirected to login

Sessions expire after a while. Sign in again; your workspaces keep running in the meantime.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Groups represent teams or departments. They provide shared storage access and can be added as members to multiple projects.

Access: All users can belong to groups. Groups are created by platform admins; if you need a new group, submit a Request.

docs.title: Group membership model
docs.text:
A group has three roles. Your group role also determines your default permissions on projects owned by that group.

Role Add / remove members Set storage permissions Access group storage Admin ✅ ✅ ✅ Manager ❌ ✅ ✅ User ❌ ❌ ✅

Teaching assistants usually need Admin

Setting students' storage permissions only needs Manager, but adding and removing members needs Admin. If you run a course, ask a platform admin for the Admin role.

docs.title: Groups list page
docs.text:
Figure 1: Groups list showing group cards.

Each group card shows a group icon, the group name, its description, its ID, and the created date. Click the card to open the group. Platform admins also see two icon buttons on the card, Edit group and Delete group.

Group policies (Storage Policy, Build Registry Lane, Root Containers, Allowed host paths) are set by platform admins under Admin → Groups and do not appear on the card.

docs.title: View a group
docs.text:
Click any group card to open its detail page. The detail page shows:

  1. Members tab — all group members with their roles
  2. Storage tab — volumes owned by this group and their permission settings

docs.title: Requesting a new group
docs.text:
Regular users cannot create groups; the Create Group button is visible to platform admins only. If you need a new group:

  1. Go to Requests → New Request.
  2. Describe what the group is for, who will be in it, and how much group storage you need.
  3. A platform admin reviews the request, creates the group, and makes you its group admin.

docs.title: Join a group
docs.text:
Group membership is managed by group admins or platform admins. To join a group:

  1. Submit a request via Requests and select the type Access Request.
  2. Describe which group you need access to and why.
  3. A group admin or platform admin reviews the request and adds you.

No public browsing

You cannot browse or search public groups. Ask your team which group to join.

docs.title: Add members to a group
docs.text:
Requires Group Admin role.

  1. Open the group and click + Add Members (top-right of Members tab).
  2. Search for users by username or email.
  3. Select users from the results list.
  4. Click Add Members to confirm.

To add a whole class at once, use Paste users: paste the list into the text box (separated by newlines, commas, semicolons, or tabs) and click Resolve Users.

The results table lists only users who are not already members, so paging through the results never shows existing members or blank pages.

Figure 2: Add members dialog with user search and selection.

docs.title: Storage permission inheritance
docs.text:
Group permissions are set on the group page and shown read-only inside each project.

Key rule: If you are a group member, your storage permissions on a project-bound volume always come from the group; they cannot be overridden at the project level. Project-level grants exist only for direct project members who are not in the owning group. Inherited rows appear read-only on the project storage page, with a badge linking to the group permissions page.

Permissions only apply to current group members: leaving the group removes your access immediately.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
I can see a group but can't add members.

Adding members requires the Group Admin role. Ask your current group admin or a platform admin to raise your role.

Why are my storage permissions greyed out on the project page?

You are a member of the group that owns this storage, so your permissions are managed at the group level. Open the group's Storage tab to see your effective permissions.

Can I belong to more than one group?

Yes. Group memberships are independent of one another, and there is no limit on how many you can join.

How do I leave a group?

Ask a group admin or platform admin to remove you; self-removal is not supported. You lose access to that group's storage immediately; anything in your personal storage is unaffected.

docs.title: Home dashboard
docs.text:
The Home dashboard shows GPU availability, your quota usage, your running jobs, and your recent requests.

Access: all signed-in users.

docs.title: Widget reference
docs.text: Widget What it shows Refresh GPU Availability Card Free vs. allocated GPU units across the platform, plus a preemptible-queue count On page load and every 10 seconds GPU Cluster Status Anonymised GPU machine cards showing how much of each GPU is in use On page load and every 10 seconds Project count (header line) Number of projects you belong to, and how many of them have a plan On page load and every 10 seconds Resource Usage History GPU/CPU/memory quota used vs. allocated for each project that has a plan, plus plan-window status On page load and every 10 seconds; countdown ticks every second Recent Activity Your 8 most recent requests On page load and every 10 seconds My GPU Jobs Your running GPU jobs with GPU share, memory, and running time On page load and every 15 seconds

docs.title: Reading GPU availability
docs.text:
The GPU Availability Card shows the current state of the GPU pool.

Figure 1: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, resource usage, and active jobs.

  1. Read the allocated / total fraction, for example 6 / 8 GPUs.
  2. Free GPUs = total − allocated. At 0 free, a new workspace waits in the queue.
  3. The card also shows a Preemptible queues count. When every GPU is busy, a higher-priority workload can still start by stopping a lower-priority workspace in a preemptible queue.
  4. Admins also see a View Reports button that opens the Audit page.

Effective GPU units

The card counts effective GPU units, not whole cards. A 1-GPU claim at 50% SM share counts as 0.5 GPU, and only while a workload is attached to it.

docs.title: GPU cluster status
docs.text:
Below the availability card, the GPU Cluster Status grid shows anonymised GPU machines:

  • A display label such as GPU node 1 and the GPU model
  • Each physical GPU, with its index and model
  • How many shares of that machine's GPUs are taken, such as 3 / 8
  • A status bar and utilisation percentage per GPU

Use the grid to find idle models before you submit a workload, or to confirm a machine has room for a fractional claim. The dashboard never shows other users' names or workload names.

docs.title: Resource usage history
docs.text:
The chart shows your usage in every project that has a plan. Projects without a plan are not listed; if none of your projects has one, the chart shows a notice instead.

  • Each bar is one project.
  • The fill shows consumed quota (GPU hours, CPU hours, or memory).
  • Each project row shows whether its resource plan is always active, closing, opening, or expired.
  • Plan-window countdowns tick every second without a page refresh.

docs.title: Recent activity
docs.text: The Recent Activity panel lists your 8 most recent requests with their tag and when you submitted them. Click View All to open the Requests page.

docs.title: My GPU jobs
docs.text:
The My GPU Jobs table lists the GPU jobs (workspaces and deployments) you have running right now. One row is one job; a job that spans several cards is one row.

Column Description Status Always Running; finished jobs are not listed Job The last 8 characters of the job ID Project Owning project GPU Effective GPU share held, and how many cards it touches Memory GPU memory held, in GiB Running How long the job has been running

The table is read-only. Open or delete a workspace on the Workspaces page; manage deployments from the project's Resources tab.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why does the availability card show 0 GPUs?

The card shows effective availability. If every compatible GPU or SM share is allocated, it shows 0. A workspace that stopped recently frees capacity within about a minute.

Recent Activity is empty. Is something wrong?

No. It only lists requests you have submitted. Submit one on the Requests page and it appears here.

My running workspace is not in the jobs table.

The table refreshes every 15 seconds. If it is still missing after the next refresh, reload the page (F5).

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Projects are the primary unit of resource allocation on the platform. Every workspace you launch consumes quota from a project, and every config file or deployment belongs to a project.

Access: All authenticated users. A personal project is automatically created for you when you register.

docs.title: Project page layout
docs.text:
Figure 1: Projects list in list view, the default.

The Projects page supports two view modes:

  • List view (default) — compact table with sortable columns
  • Grid view — cards with project name, description, member count, GPU usage bar

Toggle between views using the icons in the top-right of the toolbar.

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
Creating a project requires the manage-projects permission. If you don't have it, the New Project button is hidden and the create page redirects back to your project list. Ask an admin to create a project for you instead. A personal project is created for you automatically when you register.

  1. Click Projects in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Project (top-right button; shown only with the manage-projects permission).
  3. Fill in the project form:
Field Description Name Short identifier (alphanumeric, hyphens allowed) Group Owning group (required) Description Optional — what this project is for
  1. Click Create. The project appears in your list immediately.

Quota is assigned by an admin

A new project starts with zero GPU quota. Contact your admin or submit a Request to have a Resource Plan bound to your project.

docs.title: Project detail tabs
docs.text:
Click a project to open its detail page. The detail page includes core tabs for Overview, Config, Plan, Builds, GPU Claims, and Resources, plus role-dependent tabs such as Images, Members, Storage, and Settings.

Figure 2: Project detail page with Overview, Config, Plan, Builds, GPU Claims, Resources, and role-dependent tabs.

Tab Contents Overview Description, quota usage chart, GPU-hour budget, current plan, member list summary Config Versioned config files describing what you want to run Plan Bound resource plan, schedule window, allowed GPU models, and quota envelope Builds Project-scoped image builds, archive or Dockerfile source selection, shared queue status, and live build logs GPU Claims Reusable GPU reservations you can prepare in advance and attach to a deployment later Resources Live per-member GPU/CPU/memory usage, expandable to what each member is running Images / Members / Storage Additional tabs shown when your role allows image management, membership management, quota controls, or storage access Settings Project-wide workspace controls; see Project settings below

Role thresholds: the Storage, Images, and Settings tabs require Project Manager or above; the Members tab is visible to Project Admins only (platform admins must switch to Admin View via the avatar menu to be treated as an effective Project Admin). The platform prevents an Admin from demoting themselves, so a project can never lose its last Admin.

docs.title: Project settings
docs.text:
The Settings tab (Project Manager or above) holds controls that apply to every workspace in the project:

Field What it does Max workspace continuous runtime In seconds. A workspace that has run longer than this is stopped automatically. 0 means unlimited (the default).

Click Save Changes to apply. The limit also caps the lifetime of GPU desktops started from this project.

docs.title: Build project images
docs.text: Use the Builds tab when a project needs a container image that is not already in the allowed image list. Project Managers and Project Admins can start builds when image builds are enabled for the project. Project Members can view build status and logs. A member cannot start a build, but can delete an image artifact from a completed build that they started.

docs.title: Source options
docs.text: Source When to Use It Upload archive Upload a .tar.gz or .zip build context. Put the Dockerfile at the archive root. Dockerfile only Paste a Dockerfile directly. The platform creates a minimal build context.

docs.title: Build settings
docs.text:
Field Notes Image Name Short repository name, for example trainer-api. The final registry path is generated by the platform. Tag Optional. Leave empty for the platform default, or set a release tag such as v1.0.1. Build source Upload archive or pasted Dockerfile.

Builds are submitted to a shared queue and run one at a time. Each build gets a fixed amount of CPU, memory, and scratch space that you cannot change from the form, and that capacity does not consume your project or personal quota.

Uploaded archives are checked for unsafe paths and size limits before the build starts.

The build history shows status, source type, destination image, and live logs. Failed builds show a short summary in the table. Use the log button for the full output. If a build is retried, the log view keeps the previous attempt's failure reason before streaming the current one.

Each build row has icon actions: Cancel build while it is running (or Delete image artifact once it has produced an image), Clear saved logs, and Delete history record. Builders and project managers can clear saved logs for completed or failed builds; build history and images are left untouched. The member who started a completed build, or a project manager, can delete its image artifact. Clear my completed build images deletes every completed image artifact you created in the current project, while keeping the build history and saved logs. Repeated tag IDs are deleted once.

Delete history record removes only the history and saved logs. It does not delete the image artifact. Harbor reclaims registry storage during daily garbage collection. A recently uploaded image may need two garbage collection runs before its blobs are eligible for removal.

Project Managers can submit project image allowlist requests and remove project image allowlist entries only for projects they currently manage. Project Members can view the project's image request history, but global catalog publications and other projects' image rules remain admin-controlled.

The Images tab splits into Available and Requests. Available lists the images this project may already pull. Requests lists every image request raised for the project, pending ones first, with its status, submission time and reviewer note; the tab label carries a badge with the pending count. Submitting a request through Add switches you to that tab so the new request is visible immediately.

A request you filed yourself can be taken back with Withdraw while it is still pending; you can submit it again afterwards. Requests filed by someone else, or already approved or rejected, offer no withdraw action.

Approved-as-global requests leave the project list

When an admin approves a request and ticks Make global, the request stops being project-scoped and disappears from this tab. The image itself then appears under Available.

Build access is project-governed

If the start form is hidden, the project either does not have Image Build Permission enabled or your project role cannot start builds. Build history and logs remain visible so you can still inspect previous jobs. Ask a project manager or platform admin to adjust the project setting or your role.

docs.title: GPU Claims
docs.text: The GPU Claims tab lists GPU reservations you can prepare for a project before deploying anything. A claim reserves GPU quota the moment you create it, but only starts counting GPU-hours once it is attached to a running workload. You can pick a claim in the deploy dialog whenever a config file declares a GPU claim slot.

docs.title: Create a claim
docs.text:
Fill in the Create GPU ResourceClaim form and click Create:

Field Notes Claim name Name used when you attach this claim to a deployment. Letters, digits, and hyphens only. GPU device class The GPU model to reserve. The form defaults to a specific model; pick Any only when the model does not matter. GPU count How many physical cards this claim reserves. A multi-GPU claim stays a single reservation. SM share Compute slice from 1% to 100%. The resulting effective GPU count is shown beside the form. VRAM mode Elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads; Hard cap enforces the percentage you pick. VRAM share Used only with Hard cap. The reserved memory is derived from the smallest card of the selected model.

Every replica of a Deployment shares the same claim. A 2-GPU claim stays one 2-GPU reservation no matter how many replicas run, and quota and GPU-hours are counted once per claim rather than once per replica.

A claim that is not attached to anything uses 0 GPU-hours but still counts against project and per-user GPU quota. The table columns are Name, Owner, GPU, SM, VRAM, Status, and Allocation, plus a delete icon. Status is Reserved (created, nothing attached), Allocated (a GPU is assigned), or In use by . Unused claims can be deleted; a claim in use by a running workload cannot.

Claim ownership

Project Members can create their own claims. Project Managers can also see and delete claims belonging to other members of the project.

docs.title: Plan window countdown
docs.text:
When a project's resource plan defines a schedule window, the Plan tab shows a live countdown to the next boundary:

  • Window closes in HH:MM:SS while the window is open.
  • Window opens in HH:MM:SS when the next window is upcoming.
  • Always active if no schedule restriction is defined.

The deploy dialog shows the same countdown (Plan window closes in HH:MM:SS) with a warning that the workload may be evicted when the window closes. Once it has closed, the dialog shows Plan window has expired with a Switch to Default Queue link that moves the deploy to the default queue; this banner is for deployments only, workspaces cannot switch queue. When the window closes, workloads in plan-bound queues are stopped; if the plan is removed or stops allowing your queue, anything still waiting to start is dropped too. A project with no active plan cannot start workloads at all.

Queues may also carry a runtime limit. When the queue you selected has one, your workload is stopped automatically after that many seconds. The limit is set by an admin and cannot be raised or disabled from your config file.

The Overview tab also shows the plan's GPU-hours bar when the plan has a GPU-hour budget: allocated GPU-hours in the current period against the budget, the reset period (monthly, weekly, or every N hours, set by an administrator), and when it next resets (UTC+8). Once the budget is used up, new GPU jobs and workspaces are blocked until the reset; running jobs are unaffected.

docs.title: Config file versioning
docs.text: Every save creates a new, immutable version. Old versions are never overwritten, so you can always look back at an earlier one, or redeploy it. Edit or upload a config file, save it, and a new version appears; you can deploy any version.

docs.title: Working with config files
docs.text:
1. Go to Projects → [your project] → Config tab.
  2. Click New File to upload a YAML file or paste content in the editor.
  3. Each save creates a new version.
  4. Click the History icon next to a config to view all versions.
  5. To deploy a specific version, click Deploy on the version row.
  6. In the deploy dialog, pick the scheduling queue. If the YAML contains GPU claim slots, choose one of your reserved GPU claims for each slot for this deploy only.

Running instances appear in the project's Resources tab. A separate Deployments page at /projects/<project id>/deployments lists deployments with Personal and Members tabs; it has no sidebar link, so open it by URL.

docs.title: Containers you can shell into
docs.text:
To open a Terminal into a container, it has to stay running. A shell with no arguments, such as command: ["/bin/sh"], exits immediately, so the container restarts over and over and every terminal attempt fails.

Either give the container real work:

command: ["sleep", "infinity"]

or keep the shell alive by enabling stdin and tty under Interactive shell in the Resource Wizard (stdin: true and tty: true in raw YAML). The wizard warns you when a bare shell would exit immediately.

Once the container is running, open the project Resources tab and click Terminal on the Pod row. Deployment and Job rows have no terminal button. Expand them to reach the running instance they created.

docs.title: Deploy rules
docs.text:
Deploying, validating, inspecting, and deleting config-file instances needs the Project Manager role or higher. Quota is checked against everything you already have in flight, so a workload still waiting to start keeps holding its share until it finishes or is removed. Config files can deploy Pod, Deployment, and Job workloads; other kinds are not accepted.

Every container must set both a memory request and a memory limit of at least 128Mi; missing values are rejected during deploy and dry-run validation. Always include the unit: a bare memory: "1" means one byte and is rejected.

docs.title: Asking for a GPU
docs.text:
There are two ways a config file can ask for a GPU.

  • Inline GPU request. In the Resource Wizard, pick a GPU model in the container's resource settings. The platform counts it toward quota, checks the model against your plan's allowed models, and sets up the GPU when you deploy.
  • Reusable GPU claim. In the Resource Wizard, choose Pick at deploy and give the slot a name such as train-a. The slot name is only a label; you map it to one of your own claims from the GPU Claims tab in the deploy dialog.

Every replica of a Deployment shares one claim. If only some replicas should use a claim, split them into separate Deployments. Configs that request no GPU need no allowed-model list, and never receive a GPU claim.

Advanced: writing the YAML yourself

Leave platform-owned fields out of your YAML: do not set metadata.namespace, metadata.generateName, metadata.ownerReferences, or metadata.finalizers. For storage, use {{userVolume}} to mount your personal volume; naming a volume directly works only in group-owned projects, and only for volumes the owning group already has.

  • An inline GPU request goes straight into the container's resource requests, for example nvidia.com/rtx6000: "1".
  • A GPU claim slot is an annotation on the Pod, or on the Deployment's template: platform-go/dra-claim-name: '{{ gpuClaimName "train-a" }}'. {{gpuClaimName}} with no name still works as the default slot. Two workloads can share a slot deliberately, or use different slots to get different claims.

Config files and deployments require Project Manager role

Only project members with Manager or higher role can create, edit, deploy, validate, inspect, or delete config-file instances.

docs.title: Managing members
docs.text:
1. Open the project and go to the Members tab.
  2. Click + Add Members (requires Project Admin role).
  3. Search for users by username or email.
  4. Select a role for each user:
Role What they can do User Launch workspaces, view configs Manager Edit configs, manage deployments Admin Add/remove members, set member quotas
  1. Click Confirm to save.

Project Admins can select several rows at once to remove members, change roles, or set per-user quotas in bulk. Managers and Admins can see everyone's quota; a Project User sees only their own. A quota of 0 means that resource is unlimited for that member, still capped by the project plan.

Group-inherited members. Members who joined through the owning group can be included in a bulk quota change, but not in bulk remove or role changes; their membership and role are managed in the group instead.

Removing a direct member also removes their workspace area in the project, any project storage permission overrides, and their per-user quota. Group-inherited members must be removed from the owning group instead.

docs.title: Group inheritance and effective project role
docs.text:
When a project is owned by a group, the platform resolves each caller's effective project role as follows:

  1. If the user has an explicit project member record, that role wins (admin / manager / user).
  2. Otherwise, for personal projects, the personal owner is treated as admin.
  3. Otherwise, the user's group role in the owning group is used as the effective project role. A Group Admin therefore acts as a Project Admin on every project owned by that group, even without being added to the project directly.

This is why a Group Admin can set per-user quotas on a project owned by their group, and see the batch selection controls in the Members tab, without being added as a direct member.

Offboarding tip: when someone leaves the lab, ask an admin to remove them from the owning group. Access to every project joined through that group disappears automatically, with no per-project cleanup.

docs.title: Deleting a project
docs.text:
Only a platform admin can delete a project, from Admin → Projects. There is no delete action on the project page. Ask an admin, or submit a Request; delete the project's workspaces first. Effects:

  • Config version history and deployment records are permanently removed.
  • Storage volumes are not deleted (they remain on the Storage page).

docs.title: Resources tab
docs.text:
The Resources tab summarizes live usage by project member:

Column Meaning User Project member GPU Effective GPU units currently used CPU Requested or observed CPU cores Memory Memory in MiB Pod (the running instance) How many that member currently has running

Project Admins, Project Managers, and platform Admin/Manager roles see every project member; regular Project Users see only their own row. Expand a row to inspect what is running, or terminate the resources you are allowed to manage. Terminating a workload here releases the quota it was holding.

For Pod rows, hover, focus, or tap the status badge to see recent events. This helps when a workload looks like it is still starting but is really failing to pull its image.

docs.title: GPU quota overview
docs.text:
The Overview tab shows a quota bar for each resource type:

Resource What It Tracks GPU Effective GPU units consumed vs. plan limit CPU CPU cores consumed by running workspaces Memory RAM consumed by running workspaces

If the GPU bar is full (100%), new workspace launches will queue and wait for resources to free up.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
I don't see a New Project button.

The button is shown only to users with the manage-projects permission. If you don't have it, ask an admin to create a project for you. Your personal project is created automatically when you register.

How do I view old config file versions?

On the Config tab, click the clock icon (History) next to any config file to see all past versions with their timestamps.

My project quota is 0 GPUs. How do I get more?

Submit a Resource Request via Requests. An admin will review and bind a Resource Plan to your project.

What's the difference between a workspace's GPU and a GPU Claim?

A workspace reserves its GPU only for as long as the workspace exists. A GPU Claim is a standalone reservation that survives across deployments. Use one when several jobs need the same fractional GPU and you want to avoid rescheduling churn.

Why is the Deploy button disabled?

Either the project has no active plan bound, or the plan window is currently closed and only the default queue is selectable. Check the Plan tab for the next opening time.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
Use a request to ask platform administrators for something: more GPU quota, new storage, access to a group or an image, a feature, or to report a bug.

Access: all signed-in users.

docs.title: Request types
docs.text: Type When to use it Resource More GPU/CPU quota, more storage, or a new allocation Access Join a group, reach a shared storage volume, or get a higher role Feature Suggest a platform feature Bug Report a platform problem Question Ask the administrators something Other Anything else

docs.title: Request states
docs.text: State What it means What you can do Pending Submitted, waiting for an admin Add details in the message thread Processing An admin is working on it Answer admin questions in the thread Completed Resolved; the thread is closed Open a new request if you need more Rejected Declined Read the reason and submit a new request; an admin can also reopen it

docs.title: Submit a request
docs.text:
1. Click Requests in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Request (top right).

Figure 1: New request form with request tag, subject, and description.

  1. Fill in the form:
Field Description Project Optional. Link the request to one of your projects so admins see its current GPU quota; the project's GPU bar appears next to the picker. Request Tag Pick one: Resource, Access, Feature, Bug, Question, Other. Subject One line, for example "4 GPU units for project LLM-Training". Description Rich text with formatting, code blocks, and inline images. Drag screenshots in. Inline images: JPEG, PNG, GIF, or WebP, up to 10 MiB each.
  1. Click Submit Request. The request starts as Pending. There are no drafts.

Say why, how much, how long

For a resource request, name the project, the number of GPUs, the period, and the research goal. Admins decide on that.

docs.title: My requests
docs.text:
Figure 2: Requests list with type tags, status badges, and creation dates.

The Requests page lists everything you have submitted: request tag, status badge, subject, and creation date. Click a request to open its message thread.

docs.title: Message thread
docs.text:
1. Click the request card.
  2. Type in the box at the bottom.
  3. Click Post Reply. Admin replies appear in the same thread.

Figure 3: Request detail page with the message thread.

docs.title: Image requests
docs.text:
When the base image you need is not on the platform allowlist, use the Request Image form (from the project Images tab or the image catalog). Some projects are allowed to use any image; if yours is one of them, you can skip this form.

Field Description Registry Optional. Defaults to docker.io. Repository Image path without the tag, for example pytorch/pytorch, or nvidia/* for a whole family. Tag Optional. Defaults to latest, or * when the repository is a wildcard.

A live preview shows the exact image reference the admin will review. Once approved, the image appears in the workspace and deploy forms.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
How long does review take?

Most requests are handled within 1–2 business days. After three days without a reply, follow up in the thread.

Can I edit or cancel a request?

No. Add or correct details in the thread. After Completed the thread closes; open a new request instead.

My request was rejected. Can I resubmit?

Yes. Read the reason, adjust, and submit a new one. Mention the previous request number.

I got no notification when my request was resolved.

Turn on Push Notifications under Settings → Notifications.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
On the Settings page you update your profile, change your password, manage API tokens for the CLI, set notifications, and pick the display language.

Access: all signed-in users. Open Settings in the left sidebar (Infrastructure section).

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
Figure 1: Settings page with the Profile, Security, Notifications, and Preferences tabs.

Tab What you do there Profile Edit your full name; see your username and email Security Change your password; create and revoke API tokens; copy CLI setup commands Notifications Turn notifications on or off Preferences Choose the display language

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
• Full Name — editable; shown wherever your name appears
  • Username — read-only; your sign-in name

  • Email — read-only when your account comes from the account directory

  • Open the Profile tab.

  • Edit Full Name.
  • Click Save Changes.

docs.title: Change password
docs.text:
1. Open the Security tab.
  2. Enter your Current Password.
  3. Enter a New Password (at least 8 characters).
  4. Repeat it in Confirm Password.
  5. Click Change Password.

One password everywhere

The new password applies to every sign-in, including the VPN. Accounts managed by an external identity provider change their password there, not here.

docs.title: API tokens and CLI
docs.text:
The Security tab is also where you get credentials for cscc-cli.

The token table lists every active token on your account with its prefix, last-used time, and expiry.

  • Create token — creates a token with an optional name. The full value is shown once; copy it before you close the dialog. The dialog also shows a ready-to-paste cscc-cli login --api-url ... --token cscc_... command.
  • Revoke — invalidates a token. CLI sessions using it fail on their next call.

Tokens last 90 days by default. You can hold at most 20 active tokens.

Shown once

The token value is never stored in readable form. If you lose it, revoke it and create a new one.

Official cscc-cli releases already trust the platform certificate, and the commands on this page already point at the right API address.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The tab has two checkboxes:

Checkbox What it does Push Notifications In-app notifications about your requests and projects. Saved when you click Save Changes. Email Notifications Shown, but not saved yet; email delivery depends on your platform's mail setup.

docs.title: Preferences
docs.text: Under Language, pick English or Traditional Chinese and click Save. The interface switches immediately.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The password fields are greyed out.

Your account is managed by an external identity provider. Change the password there.

I forgot my password.

There is no self-service reset on the sign-in page. Ask a platform admin to reset it; the new password applies everywhere, including the VPN.

My email is wrong.

Email comes from the account directory. Ask an admin to update it.

Can I delete my account?

Only an admin can. Submit a request describing what you need.

I lost my API token. Can I recover it?

No. Revoke it under Security and create a new one.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
A storage volume is a folder that survives your workspaces. Anything you write inside a mounted volume stays when the workspace stops or is deleted.

A workspace with no volume keeps nothing

Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>; each group volume mounts at /mnt/shared/<volume name>. Files written anywhere else are lost when the workspace stops, restarts, or is deleted. The platform warns you before it starts a workspace with no volume.

Access: an admin creates personal storage, so not every account has one. Check the My Storage tab on the Storage page and ask an admin if it is missing. Group admins manage access to group volumes; only current group members can hold permissions on them.

docs.title: Storage types
docs.text: Personal storage Group storage Owner You A group Created by Admin Admin, on request Who can use it You only Group members, by permission Best for Your datasets, notebooks, experiments Shared datasets, team work Managed from My Storage tab Group Storage tab

docs.title: Storage page
docs.text:
Figure 1: Storage page with the My Storage and Group Storage tabs.

  • My Storage — your own volume: a card with the file browser status (Stopped, Starting, Running, Stopping, Error) and the file browser buttons. The card shows no capacity.
  • Group Storage — volumes of the groups you belong to, as a table: name, status (Active, Available, or Lost), file browser status, capacity (for example 50Gi), access mode, your permission, group, created date, and the action icons.

Every group member sees the Permissions icon on a group volume, but only group managers and admins can open the permissions page; anyone else is sent back to the Storage page.

docs.title: Volume lifecycle
docs.text:
1. You ask for storage on the Requests page.
  2. An admin approves and creates the volume.
  3. The volume is bound to a project and appears in the workspace form.
  4. Your workspace mounts it. Data survives restarts.
  5. An admin deletes it. The volume and its data are gone.

Deletion is permanent

Deleting a volume destroys everything in it. Back up what matters before you ask for removal.

docs.title: Browse files
docs.text:
1. On the My Storage tab, click Start FileBrowser; wait until the badge shows Running.
  2. Click Open FileBrowser. The browser opens in a new tab.
  3. When you are done, click Stop FileBrowser.

On a group volume, use the icons in the Actions column: Start FileBrowser, then Browse, then Stop FileBrowser. When your permission on that volume is None, these icons are hidden.

Figure 2: File browser with upload, download, and delete.

In the browser you can navigate folders, upload (drag and drop or file picker), download files and folders, create folders, and delete. Deletions are immediate.

Large uploads

For files over 500 MB, download them inside a workspace with wget, curl, or rclone instead of uploading through the browser, which has size and timeout limits.

docs.title: Mount storage in a workspace
docs.text:
1. In the New Workspace form, find the Storage Volumes section. It lists your personal storage and the group volumes bound to the selected project.
  2. Tick the volumes you want.
  3. Click Start.

Mount paths are fixed: personal storage at /home/<your username>, each group volume at /mnt/shared/<volume name>.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Group volumes have a per-user permission:

Permission What you can do Read Mount and read Write Mount, read, and write None Nothing; you cannot mount or browse it

A None set by a group admin wins over anything the project or group would otherwise grant; clearing it restores your normal permission. Ask your group admin for changes. Group admins edit permissions in bulk on the group's Storage tab (see Groups).

docs.title: Ask for more storage
docs.text:
Platform admins create group volumes; a group admin role cannot. To get one, or more capacity:

  1. Go to Requests → + New Request.
  2. Pick type Resource.
  3. Describe what you need: size, purpose, group name.
  4. Click Submit. An admin reviews it and creates the volume.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
My volume shows Pending. When can I use it?

It is still being created, usually under a minute. After 5 minutes, contact an admin.

My volume is full but I see no large files.

In a workspace terminal run du -sh /home/<your username>/*. Hidden folders such as .cache and .local, and notebook checkpoints, are the usual cause.

I see a group volume but cannot browse it.

You need at least Read on that volume. Ask your group admin.

Is my data still there after I delete a workspace?

Yes. Data is lost only when the volume itself is deleted.

Can several workspaces mount the same volume?

Yes. Personal and group volumes can be mounted by several workspaces at the same time.

Files I uploaded in the browser do not show in my workspace.

Look under /home/<your username> (personal) or /mnt/shared/<volume name> (group). Volumes attach at start, but files uploaded later appear immediately; no restart needed.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is a JupyterLab or VS Code environment with GPU access, started from one of the platform's images.

Access: All project members with sufficient project quota.

docs.title: Workspace states
docs.text:
State What it means What you can do Starting The workspace is downloading its image and starting up. Wait 30–120 seconds Running The workspace is ready to use. Open or Delete Stopped The workspace is not running (for example after the idle limit or the runtime limit). Files in mounted storage are kept. Delete, then create a new one Error The workspace failed to start. Delete, then create a new one

There is no start or stop button. A workspace runs until you delete it or the platform removes it.

docs.title: Workspace list page
docs.text:
Figure 1: Workspace list with status badges.

Each row shows:

  • Workspaces — the workspace name, with the environment type and project below it
  • Status — Running (green), Starting (yellow), Stopped (grey), Error
  • Image — the image it runs
  • Resources — the GPU count, or CPU for a CPU-only workspace
  • The last activity time
  • Open (only while Running) and Delete

Below the table, a notice shows the idle limit: Auto-stop after N minutes of inactivity. Only real IDE activity (opening pages, terminal input, notebook execution) counts as activity.

docs.title: Launch a workspace
docs.text:
1. Click Workspaces in the left sidebar.
  2. Click New Workspace (top-right).

Figure 2: New workspace form with project, environment, image, GPU, and storage fields.

  1. Fill in the form:
Field Description Project The project this workspace belongs to (determines quota). Projects without a plan are marked (No Plan) and cannot start a workspace. Internet Access Read-only. A banner under the project shows whether workspaces in this project can reach the Internet (Enabled / Disabled). When disabled, the workspace still reaches platform services but cannot download from outside. Environment JupyterLab or VS Code Image One of the platform's images for that environment: Base Notebook, PyTorch, TensorFlow, CUDA Dev, and their "(Root)" variants. Images you request or build for a project are for deployments, not workspaces. Root shell Makes you root inside your own container. Shown only when the project (and, for group-owned projects, the owning group) allows root containers. Scheduling queue A radio list of the queues the project plan allows. See Scheduling queue and priority below. GPU Number of GPUs; pick No for a CPU-only workspace. GPU Model One of the models your plan allows. Models outside the plan are hidden. Compute quota (%) Share of each GPU's compute. 100% is a full GPU; smaller values count as fractional usage. When you pick a fractional GPU, this is set for you. GPU memory quota (%) Share of each GPU's memory. Leave Follow compute on to match the compute quota, or turn it off and set a separate value. Everything on one card adds up to at most 100%. CPU / Memory Optional override; defaults to plan limits Storage Volumes Tick the volumes to mount. Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>; each group volume at /mnt/shared/<volume name>.

The name is generated; there is no name field.

  1. Click Start.
  2. The workspace appears in Starting state. Wait 30–120 seconds for the workspace to download its image and start.
  3. When status changes to Running, click Open to open the IDE in a new browser tab.

No storage selected

If you have no personal storage and tick no group volume, the platform shows This workspace will not keep your files before it starts. Everything you write lives only inside the container and is lost when the workspace stops, restarts, or is deleted. Click Cancel and tick a volume, or I understand, start anyway.

Idle shutdown

Workspaces with no activity for the idle limit shown under the list are stopped automatically to free GPUs for others. Delete the stopped workspace and create a new one; files in mounted storage are kept.

Root shell

Root shell only makes you root inside your own container. It grants no access to the platform or other users' data. If the toggle is missing, ask an admin to enable root containers on the project and, for group-owned projects, the owning group.

docs.title: Scheduling queue and priority
docs.text:
Each workspace chooses a scheduling queue. Queues carry a priority value, an optional preemptible flag, and an optional deserved GPU limit set by an admin.

Concept Effect on your workspace Higher priority Scheduled before workspaces in lower-priority queues when GPUs are scarce. Preemptible queue Your workspace can be stopped to make room for a higher-priority workload. Default queue Lowest-priority fallback queue. It still requires an active project plan and must be allowed by that plan.

The launch form lists queues allowed by the project's active plan. If no plan is bound, workspace launch is rejected until an admin binds one. GPU workspaces are also checked against the GPU models your plan and queue allow, even when you leave the model field blank and the platform picks one for you.

docs.title: Plan window
docs.text:
If a project plan defines a weekly or one-off schedule window, workspaces in plan-bound queues only run while the window is open.

  • Outside the window, Start is rejected with The project's plan is not within its active time window.
  • When the window closes, workspaces running in plan-bound queues are stopped. Create a new one inside the next window.
  • A workspace cannot switch queue. The Switch to Default Queue banner exists only in the deploy dialog for deployments; see Projects.

The Home dashboard and the project's Plan tab show the window countdown.

docs.title: Connect to your workspace
docs.text:
Once a workspace is Running, click Open. The platform connects your browser straight to the workspace; no extra setup is needed.

  • JupyterLab opens at /lab, the standard Jupyter interface.
  • VS Code (code-server) opens at /, full VS Code in the browser.

Persistent work

Code and notebooks saved under /home/<your username> (personal storage) or /mnt/shared/<volume name> (group volume) survive the workspace. Files written anywhere else are lost when the workspace is deleted.

Use $XDG_CONFIG_HOME, not a hardcoded ~/.config

Workspaces ship with XDG_CONFIG_HOME=~/.local/config, so XDG-aware tools (code-server, pip config, gh, …) write their settings there and those settings persist across workspaces.

If you configure a tool by hand, use $XDG_CONFIG_HOME rather than a hardcoded ~/.config.

docs.title: Stopping a workspace
docs.text: Stopping is not available. To free the GPU, click Delete; the workspace is removed, and files in mounted storage volumes are kept. Create a new workspace when you need one again.

docs.title: Bulk delete (admins)
docs.text: Admins with workspace-management rights can tick several workspaces and delete them in bulk using the toolbar that appears when checkboxes are ticked.

docs.title: How GPUs are allocated
docs.text:
When you pick a GPU model and compute quota, the platform reserves that share of a GPU for your workspace.

  • GPU is the number of physical GPUs requested.
  • Compute quota (%) controls the effective share used for quota accounting and GPU sharing. The form shows Effective GPU so you can see what counts against your quota.
  • GPU memory quota (%) follows the compute quota unless you set it separately.
  • Quota counts every workspace you have asked for, including ones still waiting to start.
  • Use nvidia-smi inside your workspace to confirm which devices are visible.
  • For exclusive or model-specific access, select 100% and a model allowed by your plan, or ask an admin to adjust the plan.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
The Open button doesn't appear even though status is Running.

The connection can take a few extra seconds to become ready. Wait 10 seconds and refresh the page. If the button still does not appear, the workspace is probably restarting repeatedly. Check with your admin.

My workspace stopped automatically.

Workspaces with no activity for the idle limit, or past the project's runtime limit, are stopped automatically. Delete it and create a new one; files in mounted storage are kept.

I see an error status. What do I do?

Delete the workspace and create it again. Common causes: the image could not be downloaded, not enough quota, or the GPU model you asked for is unavailable. If it repeats, submit a Request.

Can I have multiple workspaces running at once?

Yes, as long as their total GPU consumption stays within your project's quota.

My workspace was evicted with reason 'Plan window expired'.

Workspaces in plan-bound queues are stopped when the schedule closes. Create a new one inside the next window.

Why are some GPU models greyed out in the launch form?

The plan attached to your project specifies an allowed GPU model list. Models outside that list are hidden. Ask a project manager to bind a plan that includes the model you need.

關於這些影片

開啟 OpenVPN Connect，匯入拿到的 .ovpn 設定檔。每台電腦只需做一次。

0:09．無聲．完整說明見快速開始

docs.title: C0-2 — 連線 VPN
docs.text:
做任何事之前先連線。沒有 VPN，儀表板網址連解析都不會成功。

關於這些影片

docs.title: L1-1 — 部署 Pod
docs.text:
最單純的工作負載。Pod 只跑一次，沒有東西會幫你重啟它，名字就是你取的那個。

docs.text:
完成數 是總共要跑幾次，平行數 是同時幾個在跑。Job 跑完就結束，Pod 和 Deployment 不會。

1:52．無聲．完整說明見專案

docs.title: L1-4 — 刪除單一 Pod（上）
docs.text:
一份設定檔就是一個可拋棄的單位。刪掉其中任何一個 Pod，就會開始清理那次部署建立的所有東西。

0:13．無聲．完整說明見專案

docs.title: L1-5 — 刪除單一 Pod（下）
docs.text:
Pod、Deployment 和 Job 會一起消失。想個別控制，就把它們分成不同的設定檔分別部署。

0:26．無聲．完整說明見專案

docs.title: L2 — 申請映像
docs.text:
專案 → 映像 分頁 → 新增 → 填 Registry / Repository / Tag → 提交申請。畫面會切到 申請紀錄，讓你確認確實送出了。

1:12．無聲．完整說明見專案

docs.title: L3 — 自己建置映像
docs.text:
專案 → 建置 分頁 → 上傳壓縮檔或貼上 Dockerfile → 開始建置，然後看即時日誌。全平台共用一條佇列，一次只建一個。

1:42．無聲．完整說明見專案

docs.title: L5 — 保留 GPU Claim
docs.text:
預先建立 GPU Claim，部署時再選用。SM % 是切分單張卡的算力，不是要幾張卡。

1:19．無聲．完整說明見專案

docs.title: 修課學生
docs.text:
看完從這裡開始之後，這兩段涵蓋修課作業通常還會用到的部分。

關於這些影片

這些是沒有旁白的短片段，每段上方的文字就是說明。

docs.title: S4 — 用完刪除工作區
docs.text:
沒有停止按鈕。刪除 會移除工作區；個人與群組儲存空間裡的檔案都還在，下次再建一個新的工作區。影片示範刪除流程。

docs.title: S5 — 部署一個 Pod
docs.text:
專案 → 設定 分頁 → 新檔案 → 資源精靈 → + Pod → 填映像與資源 → 建立，然後 部署。不用手寫 YAML。

docs.title: 助教
docs.text:
在平台上帶一門課：哪些是你自己來、哪些要走申請，以及一個學期怎麼開始和結束。

docs.title: T0 — 助教能做什麼、不能做什麼
docs.text:
助教是群組管理員，不是平台管理員。你的主場是群組的 存儲 分頁；建立群組、建立儲存、核准映像都要走申請。

docs.title: T1 — 申請群組與群組儲存
